passage:
Saturday
Today Aditi and I did a coin-toss contest on the balcony. Heads, she gets a biscuit; tails, I get one. It came heads FIVE times in a row! Aditi was jumping.
I said, "Now it HAS to be tails. It's my turn by law." I was so sure I bet her my two biscuits.
Heads again.
Papa laughed and said, "Good boy, but the coin doesn't remember what it did before. It has no brain." I said coins should be fair. He said fair means every toss is half and half, every single time, even after five heads.
I still think tails is coming. I'll try again tomorrow.
Chirag

qa.q: How many times in a row did the coin come up heads?
qa.a: It came heads five times in a row.

qa.q: Why was Chirag so sure the next toss HAD to be tails?
qa.a: Chirag felt confident that after five heads the coin owed him a tails to even things out, as if chance keeps score.

qa.q: What could Chirag try tomorrow to test his idea?
qa.a: He could write down lots of tosses and look at what comes after every run of heads, to see whether tails is really due.

qa.q: How did the contest feel for Aditi?
qa.a: Aditi was jumping with joy at five heads, and winning Chirag's two biscuits as well must have made it a lucky day. 😊

grounding: A boy tossing a coin with Aditi believes tails is owed after five heads and bets on it.

passage:
Under the neem tree near the bus stand, Siddharth and Pradeep were tossing a one-rupee coin to decide who would bat first in their evening game. Pradeep kept calling heads and kept winning. Five heads in a row.
"Sixth time, I'm calling tails," Siddharth announced, rolling up his sleeves. "It's overdue. The coin will want to balance."
Pradeep grinned. "Coins don't want anything."
"Everything evens out. Dadi says so about the rain too."
The coin spun, flashed in the sun, and landed in the dust. Heads.
Siddharth stared at it. "Then it must be tails next. Definitely."
Pradeep had already picked up the bat.

qa.q: What were Siddharth and Pradeep tossing the coin to decide?
qa.a: Who would bat first in their evening game.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel tails is 'overdue'?
qa.a: Siddharth feels confident because he believes things even out, as Dadi says about the rain, so five heads feel like a debt the coin must repay. 🤔

qa.q: After the sixth heads, what could help Siddharth see that each toss starts fresh?
qa.a: He could ask himself why the coin would remember the last five, or the two could toss many times and see heads and tails come in uneven runs.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the five heads?
qa.a: To Pradeep they are just lucky tosses; the coin owes nobody anything, and batting first is what matters now.

grounding: A village boy insists tails is overdue after five heads because he thinks chance balances itself.

passage:
In Ms Lindqvist's Grade 5 class in Vancouver, everyone was doing a coin experiment and recording the results. Hiroshi and Astrid shared a coin. Five heads in a row landed on their desk.
Hiroshi leaned over the tally sheet. "Next one's tails. It has to be. Five heads is too many."
"Why?" asked Astrid.
"Because it's supposed to be half and half. So now it'll catch up."
He wrote T in pencil before tossing, very lightly, just in case. Heads.
Astrid tapped the sheet. "Maybe it doesn't know it's supposed to catch up."
Hiroshi rubbed out the T and frowned at the coin, turning it over as if checking for a trick.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi write before tossing?
qa.a: He wrote T in pencil, very lightly.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Hiroshi that the coin will 'catch up'?
qa.a: Hiroshi feels confident because he knows coins land half and half overall, so he expects the coin to fix the run of heads right away, as if it remembers.

qa.q: How could Ms Lindqvist use the class tallies to help Hiroshi?
qa.a: She could gather every pair's results and show what came after runs of heads, so Hiroshi sees tails isn't more likely then.

qa.q: What would change if Astrid had agreed with Hiroshi instead of asking 'Why?'
qa.a: Hiroshi would feel even surer, and the pair might never question the idea that the coin remembers.

grounding: A boy in a coin experiment expects tails to catch up after five heads, believing chance balances itself.

passage:
Rain drummed on the tin roof of the junior hostel in Kalimpong, so study hour moved to the common room. Pema, nine, and Varun were meant to be doing maths. Instead they were tossing a one-rupee coin into a steel plate.
"Heads. Heads again. That's five," Varun counted.
Pema slapped the table. "Then tails is sure now. The coin has to even out." He bet his Sunday sweets on tails.
The warden, Mr Lepcha, stopped by. "Does the coin remember the last toss?"
"Coins can't remember," Pema said. "But five heads is too many. It will fix itself."
The coin clattered. Heads.
Pema stared at it. "Okay, NOW tails is really due."
Mr Lepcha pulled out a chair. "Let's toss it fifty times and write each one down."

qa.q: What did Pema bet on tails?
qa.a: He bet his Sunday sweets on tails.

qa.q: How does Pema feel about the next toss, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pema feels excited and certain that tails is due, slapping the table and betting his Sunday sweets even while admitting coins can't remember.

qa.q: What choice did Mr Lepcha make that could help Pema, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Tossing the coin fifty times and writing each result down lets Pema see for himself that streaks happen and the next toss doesn't correct them.

qa.q: How might Varun see Pema's bet after the sixth heads?
qa.a: Varun, who was counting the heads, might find Pema's "NOW tails is really due" funny, or might start believing it too and happily keep the Sunday sweets bet going.

grounding: It shows a boy who, after five heads, insists tails must come because he feels the coin has to balance itself out.

passage:
I'm Alka, and I'm writing this for my Class 9 observation diary. Our train to Amritsar was two hours late, so my brother Sehaj, eight, and our neighbour's daughter Jasleen started tossing a coin on the platform bench. Jasleen chose heads every time. It came up heads five times.
Sehaj started bouncing. "Now it's tails. Definitely. The coin has to be fair, so it owes me." He even asked Jasleen to bet her peanut packet.
I couldn't tell if he truly believed it or just wanted to win, but he sounded completely sure. The sixth toss was heads. He said the coin was "cheating" and checked both sides.
Later, on the train, I asked him how the coin could know what came before. He was quiet, then said, "It felt like it should."

qa.q: How many times did the coin come up heads before Sehaj said tails was definite?
qa.a: It came up heads five times.

qa.q: How does Sehaj feel about the coin, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sehaj feels excited and completely sure, bouncing and saying the coin owes him tails, then frustrated when heads comes again and he calls the coin "cheating".

qa.q: What choice did Alka make on the train, and why could it help Sehaj?
qa.a: Alka asked him how the coin could know what came before, which lets Sehaj think it through himself instead of just being told he is wrong.

qa.q: What is it like for Jasleen when Sehaj asks for the peanut packet as a bet?
qa.a: Jasleen, who kept winning with heads, may feel pressured or puzzled, since Sehaj is suddenly so sure the next toss belongs to him.

grounding: It shows a boy convinced that after five heads the coin owes him tails, as if chance remembers and balances out.

passage:
Sunday
Nikita didi and I tossed a coin to decide who gets the TV remote. I always call tails. It was heads. Then heads again. Then heads, heads, heads. FIVE heads in a row! I said, "Okay, the next one HAS to be tails. The coin owes me." Didi laughed and said, "The coin doesn't remember anything." I said that's impossible, it's been heads five times, it has to balance. She tossed. HEADS. Six!
I was so annoyed I went to my room. Then I tossed the coin by myself twenty times and wrote it down. Heads, tails, tails, heads, heads... It was all mixed up. Sometimes three the same. Sometimes not.
Maybe the coin really doesn't remember. That's kind of scary.
Tarun

qa.q: How many heads came in a row in the end?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why was Tarun sure the next toss had to be tails?
qa.a: Tarun felt the coin owed a tails after five heads, as if it would balance itself, and the sixth head left Tarun annoyed.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that helped, and what did it show?
qa.a: Tossed the coin twenty times and wrote down the results, which showed they were mixed and the coin doesn't remember past tosses.

qa.q: How does Nikita didi see the coin?
qa.a: She laughs, knowing the coin doesn't remember anything, so each toss is fresh.

grounding: A child's diary shows certainty that tails must follow five heads, as if chance has a memory.

passage: In the reading room of the village library, Jagdish and Jomon played ludo on the old wooden board every evening. That evening Jagdish hadn't rolled a six in eleven turns, and his last token was stuck at home. "Next one's a six for sure," he said, rattling the dice. "It's been waiting. It's due." "Due?" said Jomon. "The dice doesn't keep a diary." Jagdish rolled. A two. "Okay, NOW it's really due. Twelve turns!" A four. The librarian, Mr Varghese, looked over his glasses. "Jagdish, if I rolled it right now, fresh, what would my chance of a six be?" Jagdish opened his mouth, then frowned. "The same as mine?" "The same as yours on your very first turn, too." Jagdish looked at the dice as if it had tricked him. Then he rolled a six.

qa.q: How many turns had Jagdish gone without a six at first?
qa.a: Eleven turns.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish feel a six was due?
qa.a: He felt impatient and sure the dice would make up for the missing sixes, as if it remembered the long wait.

qa.q: How did Mr Varghese's question help?
qa.a: Asking what the chance would be on a fresh roll showed Jagdish that every roll has the same chance, whatever came before.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the dice?
qa.a: Jomon jokes that the dice doesn't keep a diary, seeing each roll as fresh.

grounding: A boy is sure a six is due after many turns without one, believing the dice remembers.

passage: At the school fair in Nairobi there was a spinning wheel with red and black slices, and every spin cost one token. Jamal watched it land on red four times in a row. "Black is coming," he told his sister Wanjiru. "It has to. Red's had its turn." He put all five of his tokens on black. Red. "That's five reds! Now black is super due." Wanjiru held his arm before he could spend the tokens she had given him for the cake stall. "Jamal, does the wheel know what it did before?" He stopped. The wheel was just painted wood and a pointer. "No..." "So every spin is like the first spin." Jamal looked at his empty hands, then at the cake stall, and let her lead him there.

qa.q: How many tokens did Jamal put on black?
qa.a: All five of his tokens.

qa.q: Why did Jamal believe black was super due?
qa.a: He felt excited and certain the wheel had to balance after so many reds, as if it remembered its turns.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped him spending the cake tokens and asked if the wheel knew what it did before, showing every spin is fresh.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru have felt watching Jamal bet?
qa.a: She was probably worried and a little protective, holding his arm to save the cake-stall tokens.

grounding: A boy at a fair is sure black is due after a run of reds, believing the wheel balances itself.

passage: In the Class 5 maths period at the Nashik school, Arohi ma'am handed out coins for a probability experiment. "Flip ten times and write down each result." Divyansh flipped. Heads. Heads. Heads. Heads. Heads. The whole bench leaned in. "Next one has to be tails," Divyansh announced. "It's been heads too many times. It has to balance." He was so sure he bet his friend an eraser. He flipped. Heads again. "No way!" Arohi ma'am came over. "Divyansh, does the coin remember the last five flips?" He looked at the coin. "It... doesn't have a brain." "So what are the chances for the next flip?" He thought hard. "Half and half. Same as always." He handed over the eraser, grumbling, but grinning a little.

qa.q: How many heads did Divyansh flip in a row before the sixth flip?
qa.a: Five heads.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh so sure the next flip would be tails?
qa.a: He felt excited and certain that the coin had to balance itself after so many heads, as if chance had a memory.

qa.q: How did Arohi ma'am help Divyansh see his mistake?
qa.a: She asked whether the coin remembers the last flips, which led him to see each flip is half and half on its own.

qa.q: How might the friend who won the eraser feel?
qa.a: The friend was probably pleased and amused, since Divyansh had been so sure.

grounding: Shows a child believing tails must come after five heads because chance balances itself out, until his teacher asks whether the coin remembers.

passage:
Monday. In the gully cricket match, Gautam lost the toss with heads. He called heads again on Tuesday and lost. "Tomorrow tails is due," Bhupen said. "No," said Gautam. "Heads is due. It's been tails twice."
Wednesday. Tails again. Gautam kicked the stumps. Three tails! He was sure the coin was now "full of tails" and heads had to come.
Friday. Bhupen's elder brother, home from college, watched Gautam call. "Heads, it's due!" Tails. Gautam groaned. The brother picked up the coin and flipped it twenty times on the step, counting out loud. Heads, tails, tails, heads, heads, heads... It came out eleven and nine. "It doesn't keep a list," he said. "Every flip is new." Gautam stared at the coin, then called tails, just to see.

qa.q: How many times did the brother flip the coin on the step?
qa.a: Twenty times, and it came out eleven and nine.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling on Wednesday when tails came again?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and sure that heads had to come next, kicking the stumps because the coin wasn't balancing out.

qa.q: What did the brother's experiment show, and how could Gautam use it?
qa.a: That the coin doesn't keep a list and every flip is new; Gautam can stop expecting a result to be due.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see the tosses early in the week?
qa.a: Bhupen also thinks a result can be due, just picking tails instead of heads.

grounding: Shows over a week a child believing heads must come after several tails, as if chance remembers and balances itself.

passage: Raghav, you've flipped that coin nine times and you're sure the next one must be tails? Let your Farhan Dada tell you about the marble game in our lane in Bhopal, when I was your age. We played odds and evens with a fistful of marbles. My friend always guessed. Seven times in a row, it was evens. I was certain the next had to be odds. "It's due!" I said. I bet my best cat's-eye marble. Evens. I bet two more. Evens again. By evening I had lost my whole tin. I went home crying. My father laughed and asked, "Did the marbles know what happened yesterday?" I said no. "Then why should today care?" So tell me, Raghav, does your coin remember?

qa.q: What did young Farhan bet first?
qa.a: His best cat's-eye marble.

qa.q: What was young Farhan feeling when he said "It's due!"?
qa.a: He felt certain and eager, sure that after seven evens an odd had to come.

qa.q: Which moment in the story taught young Farhan something?
qa.a: When his father asked whether the marbles knew what happened yesterday, showing that each round had no memory.

qa.q: How might Farhan's friend have seen the marble game that evening?
qa.a: The friend probably felt lucky and pleased, winning a whole tin while Farhan kept betting on what was due.

grounding: An elder recalls believing odds had to come after a long run of evens, betting and losing his marbles because chance has no memory.

passage:
The Sankranti kites were stuck on the roof because the wind had died, and the power had gone out in the whole colony. Pradeep and Jatin sat on the terrace steps with one old rupee coin.
"Heads," Jatin said, catching it. "Again." Heads. Heads. Heads. Heads.
"Five heads," Pradeep said, wide-eyed. "Now it has to be tails. It's tails's turn."
"Bet?"
"Bet my blue kite." Pradeep was completely sure. The coin had been unfair for so long that it owed tails.
Jatin flipped. Heads.
Pradeep grabbed the coin and turned it over, checking for two heads. It had a tail. "That's not possible!"
"Flip it yourself," Jatin said.
Pradeep flipped it ten more times while the sun went down. Four heads, six tails, in no pattern at all.

qa.q: How many heads came in a row before Pradeep's bet?
qa.a: Five heads came in a row.

qa.q: Why was Pradeep so sure the next flip would be tails?
qa.a: Pradeep felt confident, even excited, because after five heads the coin seemed to owe tails, as if it remembered and had to be fair.

qa.q: What could Pradeep learn from the ten extra flips?
qa.a: Pradeep could notice the heads and tails came in no pattern, so each flip starts fresh, and stop betting on a turn being due.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the coin game?
qa.a: Jatin seems amused and calm, happy to win the kite and letting Pradeep test the coin with ten more flips.

grounding: Shows a child who believes tails must come after five heads because chance should balance itself.

passage:
It was Christmas week, and Farida's flat had a paper star in the window and a snakes-and-ladders board on the floor.
Suraj had rolled eleven times without a six. Farida had rolled three sixes already and was near the top.
"Now it's coming," Suraj announced, shaking the dice extra long. "Eleven times, no six. The dice has to give me one now. It's only fair."
"The dice doesn't know," Farida said.
"It knows. It's been saving it."
He rolled. A one. Straight onto the snake at 17.
Suraj flopped back onto the carpet. "That's cheating!"
Farida's grandmother, watching from the sofa with a slice of plum cake, laughed. "Beta, I've been waiting for a six my whole life. The dice never once felt sorry for me."

qa.q: How many times had Suraj rolled without a six?
qa.a: Suraj had rolled eleven times without a six.

qa.q: Why did Suraj feel sure a six was coming?
qa.a: Suraj felt certain and hopeful, believing the dice had been 'saving' a six and owed him one after eleven rolls.

qa.q: What could Suraj try to test the idea about the dice?
qa.a: Suraj could roll many times and write down the numbers, to see that a six doesn't get likelier just because it is late.

qa.q: How does Farida's grandmother see Suraj's complaint?
qa.a: She finds it funny and gently teases that the dice never felt sorry for her either, showing it has no memory.

grounding: Shows a child who believes a six must come after a long run without one, as if the dice balances itself out.

passage:
"Five tosses in a row, Vikas bhaiya. Five! All heads."
"So?"
"So tomorrow I'm calling tails. It has to come. The coin's used up all its heads."
Vikas wiped mango juice off his chin; it was the middle of the summer holidays. "A coin doesn't have a tank of heads, Zubin."
"It does. It's like... it balances."
"Okay. Toss it ten times and tell me after each toss if tails is getting more likely."
Zubin tossed. "Heads." Again. "Tails." "Tails." "Heads." "Heads." "Heads."
"Three heads in a row," Vikas said. "Is tails due now?"
"...Yes?"
"And if it's heads again?"
Zubin chewed his lip. "Then it's more due."
"Or," Vikas said, "the coin just does what it does. Every toss, fifty-fifty. Call whatever you like at the cricket camp tomorrow and think about your batting order."

qa.q: How many tosses in a row came up heads before the talk?
qa.a: Zubin said five tosses in a row came up heads.

qa.q: Why does Zubin feel sure tails will come tomorrow?
qa.a: Zubin feels confident that the coin has used up its heads and must balance out, so tails seems owed.

qa.q: What small test does Vikas suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Tossing ten times and asking after each toss whether tails is getting likelier shows Zubin that every toss stays fifty-fifty.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Zubin's plan for the toss?
qa.a: Vikas finds it harmless but wants Zubin to stop fretting about the toss and think about the batting order.

grounding: Shows a child who believes a coin must turn up tails after a run of heads, because chance should even out.

passage: It was the last day of the Diwali holidays, and Hafsa and I were flipping a one-rupee coin on the terrace to decide who got the last laddoo. Heads for her, tails for me. Heads. Heads again. Heads, heads, heads. Five heads in a row! "Now it has to be tails," I said. "The coin knows it owes me." I made her flip once more, then again, sure each time that tails was coming. Heads. Tails. Heads. "Best of twenty?" I begged. Hafsa laughed so hard she dropped the coin. "Vishal, the coin doesn't remember anything!" I still think that coin was cheating. But we split the laddoo in half.

qa.q: How many heads came in a row?
qa.a: Five heads in a row.

qa.q: Why was Vishal so sure tails had to come next?
qa.a: After five heads it felt fair and certain that the coin owed a tails, so Vishal felt hopeful and impatient, as if chance kept score.

qa.q: What could help Vishal understand the coin?
qa.a: Flipping it many times and writing down each result would show that every flip starts fresh, whatever came before.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Vishal's idea?
qa.a: Hafsa finds it very funny, because to her the coin doesn't remember anything 😄

grounding: Shows a child sure tails must come after five heads, as if chance has a memory and balances itself.
